summary: For ages 9–11, teach the extrapolation-and-test cycle in fair testing: read the trend in an existing set of results, use it to make a specific, testable prediction for a NEW untested value or condition, design a fresh fair test to check that prediction, and explicitly state the reasoning that connects the original data to the prediction. The distinctive skill is turning a one-off experiment into an iterative line of enquiry, while learning that an extrapolated prediction is a claim to be tested, not a proven fact.
misconceptions: Making a prediction as a random guess rather than reading it off the existing trend in the data.
Treating an extrapolated prediction as a proven fact instead of a claim that still needs its own fair test.
Assuming a pattern continues indefinitely beyond the tested range (e.g. that a trend never levels off or reverses) without checking.
Skipping the reasoning link — stating a prediction without connecting it to the specific results that motivate it.
Believing an experiment 'ends' at its conclusion, rather than that good results generate the next testable question.

activities.title: Predict a new point, then run the test to check it
steps: Study a graph of results from a completed fair test (e.g. sugar dissolving faster in warmer water, or distance a car rolls from three ramp heights).
Point to the trend in the data in words ('as temperature increased, dissolving got faster') before predicting anything.
Extend the trend line to a temperature/height you never tested and lock in a specific predicted value for that new condition.
Type or say the reasoning: 'I predict ___ BECAUSE the results showed ___' — before any test is run.
Run a fresh fair test at that new value, keeping everything else the same and taking repeat readings, and place the measured point on the graph next to your prediction.
Compare predicted vs measured: discuss when the point lands on your extended line, and what it means when a case makes the trend level off or change instead.
activities.insight: Good data lets you make an evidence-based prediction for conditions you have not yet tested, but an extrapolated prediction is a claim that must be checked with its own fair test — the pattern may not continue indefinitely, so science is a loop where each result raises the next question.

activities.title: Interpolation vs extrapolation: where is the prediction, and how sure are we?
steps: On a results graph, mark predictions that fall BETWEEN tested points (interpolation) and predictions that fall BEYOND the tested range (extrapolation).
For each prediction, state whether it is interpolation or extrapolation and rate how certain you can be, explaining why extrapolated predictions carry more uncertainty.
Choose which of several written predictions is best justified by the given data, and explain what makes the others weaker (guess, restated data, or unsupported leap).
Sequence the enquiry cards into the cycle: question → fair test → results → prediction → new fair test.
Say why an extrapolated prediction in particular must be tested rather than assumed.
activities.insight: Predictions between tested points are generally more secure than predictions beyond the tested range; naming which kind a prediction is tells you how much it needs checking, and an extrapolated prediction especially must be tested because the pattern might not continue.

activities.title: Justify and defend your prediction in dialogue
steps: Answer a mentor's question: 'What does this data make you predict for a value you haven't tried — and why that value?'
Explain how your prediction follows FROM the observed pattern, not from a hunch.
Describe how you would set up the follow-up test so it is fair and actually checks your prediction (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings).
Respond to the challenge: 'What if the trend stops or levels off past a certain point — how would your test reveal that?'
Explain how making an evidence-based prediction differs from simply repeating what you already found.
activities.insight: Articulating and defending the evidence-to-prediction reasoning out loud is the core assessed skill; a prediction without its justification and a fair plan to check it is incomplete.

checkQuestion: You tested how far a car rolls from three ramp heights and found: the higher the ramp, the further the car rolls. A friend asks, 'So what should we try next?' Using your results, what would you predict for a ramp height you haven't tried yet — and what new test would you set up to check whether your idea holds? Talk me through your thinking.
checkAnswer: A strong response uses the pattern in the results to make a specific, testable prediction for a NEW, untried value ('an even higher ramp will roll even further, maybe about X'), and designs a fair follow-up test to check it (new height, everything else kept the same). It explains that the prediction comes FROM the observed pattern, and that a further test is needed because the pattern might not continue (it could level off) — treating the prediction as something to test, not something already proven.
